title: How to build and optimize your B2B lead generation funnel
summary: Build and optimize your B2B lead generation funnel with proven strategies, real examples, and automation tactics that scale pipeline.
body_text: It’s not uncommon for a prospect to download an ebook from a company’s website and immediately qualify as a marketing-qualified lead (MQL). If they open their first nurture email, there’s a good chance they will become a sales-qualified lead (SQL). A rep will receive a notification to follow up immediately. Scenarios like this aren’t as outlandish as you might think. Somewhere along the way, a gated asset and a five-email sequence became the default definition of a lead generation funnel. Fortunately, you don’t need to follow the same outdated playbook. Why your funnel isn’t built to convert For most teams, lead generation looks the same way: a gated content asset, a landing page to promote it, and a form that captures contact details in exchange for the download. This “funnel” usually leaves you with a list full of people who have only limited interest in your product or service. Typical lead generation funnels often share the same set of mistakes: Treating lead generation as a solely inbound marketing motion and over-relying on gated content No shared understanding between marketing and sales of what qualifies a lead as an MQL or SQL Failing to understand the target audience Casting the net too wide with the lead magnet Not having a qualification framework to segment incoming leads Adding every lead to the same nurture flow or slapping them with a pitch and never following up An average of 13 people are involved in a typical B2B buying decision, according to research by Forrester . Each stakeholder takes their own path through to an offer. They start researching different times, consume different content, and form opinions based on completely different interactions with a brand. That's not a linear buyer journey, and it exactly why most traditional funnels don't work. They follow a rigid path, target one person, and fail to support the multiple touchpoints that characterize how B2B buying actually happens. What TOFU, MOFU, and BOFU need to drive conversions Each stage of the funnel serves a prospect at a different point on their path to purchase. The content, channels, and messaging need to reflect where they are and give them what they need to move forward. TOFU: capturing attention and generating demand The top of the funnel (TOFU) is where you generate awareness among the right audience. Prospects here are either problem-aware or not yet aware of your solution. The following channels and assets create awareness at the top of the funnel: SEO and GEO content that captures anyone researching your problem category through search or AI tools before they've formed a vendor shortlist LinkedIn ads targeted by role, seniority, and company size to reach the buying committee directly Organic social that builds category authority over time Lead magnets , like reports, calculators, and templates, that offer enough standalone value to earn a form fill MOFU: nurturing interest and building trust The middle of the funnel (MOFU) is where prospects are actively evaluating options, consuming product-related content, and starting internal conversations about potential solutions. These tactics will help you stay visible and demonstrate fit at the middle of the funnel: Email nurture sequences mapped to prospect evaluation stages Webinars and live content that let prospects see your expertise in action Whitepapers and case studies that give product champions something to share internally with stakeholders you haven't reached yet Retargeting ads that keep you visible to anyone in your buying group who has already interacted with your brand Signal-based sales follow-up timed to engagement that indicates intent BOFU: turning intent into revenue The bottom of the funnel (BOFU) is where decisions get made. Prospects are comparing vendors, building business cases, and navigating internal approval processes. The following assets will help you convert buyers at the bottom of the funnel: Clear pricing pages that answer the questions a late-stage prospect is actually asking Testimonials and case studies from customers who match the prospect's profile (i.e., same industry and same use case) Demos and trials that let prospects validate fit on their own terms ROI proof the buying group can take into internal meetings without a rep in the room Direct CTAs that make the next step obvious and frictionless How to build a funnel that brings in the right people Building a funnel that brings in the right people starts with clarity. You first need to know who you're targeting, where you'll reach them, and what you'll say at subsequent stages of consideration. 1. Start with your ICP and target audience Who are you building this funnel for? Start by defining two types of buyers. Champions are the individuals who will use your product day to day and have the most to gain from it. Decision-makers care more about the business outcome the purchase drives. They don't use the tool, but they sign off on buying it. You can't target both with the same message. Start by building your funnel around the champion: their pains, their role, and the channels they use to research and solve problems. Through them, you reach the decision-maker. You can sharpen your targeting further by factoring in signals that indicate champions and decision-makers are likely to act soon. Here’s an overview of the most common buying signals: Hiring drives Funding events Tech stack changes Leadership changes Engagement with your content Tools like Artisan monitor these signals automatically and alert reps when relevant behaviors are tracked. Buyer characteristics backed by the right signals help you drive higher-quality leads into your funnel. These MQLs won’t sit at the back of your CRM forever and have a realistic chance of becoming SQLs. 2. Map your funnel across channels and touchpoints Your funnel will span more than one channel. For example, if your entry point is email, you'll need LinkedIn outreach and strong website resources (at minimum) to move leads through it. Here is a quick example of how touchpoints can map across the funnel: Outbound sequences create the opening, triggered by buying signals. Retargeting ads extend reach to the broader buying committee. SEO and GEO content captures prospects doing independent research. Email nurture keeps the champion engaged and gives them material to share internally. Your goal at this stage is to create one cohesive ecosystem with the channels in your arsenal. If you don't have the resources to connect multiple channels, don't spread yourself thin. Instead, focus on direct touchpoints like outbound outreach and precise retargeting. 3. Match messaging to each stage of the funnel Mixing messages across stages is one of the most common mistakes marketers and reps make when building B2B lead gen funnels. Pitching new leads in the first cold email ? Retargeting pipeline prospects with a top-funnel article? Running commercial PPC ads against informational intent queries? Unless you want to burn your budget, do none of these things. Meet prospects where they are. Don't rush to a pitch with someone who is early in the research phase, and don't linger with educational content when someone is ready to buy. 4. Ensure alignment on MQL and SQL definitions MQL-to-SQL transitions should never be arbitrary. They require shared criteria that both marketing and sales agree on upfront. Definitions should cover role, company size, engagement signals, and timing indicators that make a lead worth a rep's time. There are three components marketing and sales should work on together: Agree on the SQL definition upfront. Document what role, company size, engagement level, and intent signals make a lead worth a rep's time. Build a handoff workflow. When a lead hits the SQL threshold, automatically assign them to a rep with full context. The handoff should be automatic, but it needs to carry everything the next person needs to pick up where the previous account owner left off. Close the feedback loop. Review MQL-to-SQL conversion rate regularly and adjust scoring criteria accordingly. Many teams would rather build a complex workflow than have a conversation about what an SQL means to both sides. Don’t make this mistake The channels that drive B2B lead generation today Content marketing, outbound, and email aren't the only B2B lead generation channels, but they're the ones that consistently drive qualified pipeline across every funnel stage. Content captures prospects actively searching for a solution, outbound reaches the right accounts before they find you, and email keeps them moving once they’ve entered your funnel. Content that capture high-intent demand Content marketing is the practice of creating and distributing valuable, relevant content to attract and convert a clearly defined audience. Here’s an overview of different content assets and which funnel stages they serve: Organic social media (top of funnel) builds awareness and keeps your brand in front of people who aren't searching yet. SEO-focused blog posts (to p to middle of funnel) capture informational and problem-aware searches ("how to reduce churn," "what is X"). Competitor comparisons (middle to bottom of funnel) target high-intent "X vs. Y" and "X alternative" searches. Whitepapers (middle of funnel) offer depth for prospects who are evaluating an approach and need to build an internal case. Case studies (bottom of funnel) provide social proof for prospects in the decision stage. Technical documentation (bottom of funnel and post-sale) reassures technical buyers that your product does what you claim and integrates with their stack. Video demos (middle to bottom of funnel) show the product in action for prospects who want to see it work before booking a call. LinkedIn and outbound for targeted outreach Unlike content, outbound doesn't wait for prospects to find you. You reach out to them directly. Here's what an outbound workflow looks like in practice: Identify target accounts based on company-level criteria, like industry, company size, and tech stack. Build a contact list of champions and key stakeholders within those accounts whose role and seniority match your buyer profile. (Optional) Layer in intent signals like funding rounds, job postings, or website behavior to prioritize accounts and sharpen your timing. Trigger an outreach sequence across social media and email once your criteria are met. It’s possible to run an entire outbound flow on autopilot. Artisan is an AI-first platform that handles all stages of outreach from prospecting to meeting scheduling without any manual input. You simply need to define your ICP and buying signals, and AI BDR Ava, an autonomous AI employee, will take care of the rest. Email marketing and follow-up that close gaps Email marketing is how you stay in contact with prospects between touchpoints. In B2B, it does two distinct jobs depending on where the lead came from. For inbound leads, it takes the form of a nurture sequence: a series of automated emails that pick up where a prospect's last action left off. A nurture sequence feeds interested prospects with relevant content, surfaces the ones showing buying signals, and filters out those who never engage. For cold outbound leads, follow-up is what drives results. A follow-up is a second or third message to someone who didn't reply the first time, each adding a fresh angle or proof point rather than just nudging them again. What makes either work is how they respond to lead behavior. Your messaging should adjust based on each behavioral signal, like an email open or a click. Turning traffic into pipeline with better conversion paths Pushing traffic into your funnel is only part of the challenge. Converting leads into qualified sales pipeline requires the right infrastructure at every stage, from the landing page a prospect hits first to the marketing to sales handoff that leads to a sales conversation. High-converting landing pages and lead magnets Landing pages play a central role in turning traffic into leads. Every channel above, be it an SEO article, a cold email, a LinkedIn message, or a nurture sequence, eventually has to send the prospect to a landing page—a standalone page built around a single offer, like a demo, a whitepaper, or a free trial. Here’s how to optimize your lead generation landing pages for conversions: One page, one offer, one CTA: Remove navigation, secondary links, and anything that gives a visitor a reason to leave without converting. Match the message to the source: A visitor coming from a cold email about churn reduction should land on a page about churn reduction, not your homepage. Keep forms short: Name, work email, and company size are enough; you can ask for more on a sales call. Add fast loading speed, and you have a high-converting page. If you got the targeting right, of course. Smart lead capture, scoring, and CRM workflows Your lead capture, scoring, and CRM workflows are the infrastructure that keeps your lead generation funnel moving. Put the following in place before leads start coming in: Sync new records with your CRM automatically: Every new lead should create a new contact without manual data entry. Automate CRM actions: New and updated contacts should trigger relevant actions automatically, from task assignment to segment changes. Score leads: Assign an initial score the moment a lead comes in, based on the lead magnet they converted on and their firmographics. As they engage with your emails or website, their score rises, and once it crosses a set threshold, an MQL becomes an SQL. Prioritize outreach by score and signals: Reps should work the highest-scoring leads first; automated sequences should handle the rest. Examples of B2B lead generation funnels Each of these funnels works because they string together multiple coordinated touches into one repeatable motion. Pick the one that matches your go-to-market and run it consistently before adding complexity. Product-led funnel for inbound demand A prospect finds your product comparison article in search results. From there, they take an interactive demo of the product. Demo behavior triggers a targeted sales nurture sequence. Sales steps in when signals indicate a real opportunity. Webinar funnel for mid-funnel engagement A prospect registers for a webinar targeting their specific role or pain point. They attend the live event or engage with the recording. A personalized follow-up sequence reaches engaged attendees with BOFU assets. Sales steps in for prospects who have responded. Outbound-led funnel for fast pipeline A target account matches your ICP and shows a buying signal. A personalized sequence launches across email and social media. Engagement with outreach determines follow-up. Respondents are booked for a demo. How Artisan runs your funnel in the background AI is changing how sales teams build their funnels, especially when it comes to cold outreach. It's allowing them to reach more leads without increasing headcount. Artisan is an AI-first outreach platform built around an autonomous employee called Ava , who is capable of automating the whole outbound workflow right up until the point a meeting is booked. PRODUCT IMAGE (ALREADY IN CONTENTFUL): “Product Image: Pic of Ava” Ava automates all of the following parts of the lead generation workflow: Identifies accounts that match your ICP and finds contact data for the right stakeholders Enriches accounts with firmographic, technographic, and intent data Tracks funding events, job postings, and on-site behavior Launches personalized email and social media outreach once a contact meets your defined criteria Sends and adjusts follow-up messages based on prospect behavior Logs interactions and updates CRM records based on lead responses When a prospect responds, Ava keeps the conversation going until the meeting is scheduled. Your reps enter the picture only when a rep is ready to talk, allowing them to focus on real, human conversations, not busywork. Build a funnel that prints pipeline, not just leads A B2B lead generation funnel is much more than a single landing page and a nurture sequence. It's a system built around a precise ICP, mapped to how your buyers actually make decisions, and supported by the right content, channels, and automation infrastructure at every stage. Artisan allows reps to automate all of the early and middle stages of their outbound funnel. AI BDR Ava identifies your best-fit accounts and launches personalized sequences across email and social media. She then books meetings directly into your rep's calendar. Automate your outbound with an AI BDR Meet Ava—your AI BDR who handles prospecting, outreach, and follow-ups, so your team can focus on closing.

title: Piston Slap: Safely Purchasing an S63 Flagship?
summary: Anthony writes: “Hi! I am about to purchase a 2017 Mercedes S63 cabriolet with 42k miles. Is it a wise practice to drop the oils? Which oils specifically? I hear mention of adding a sacrificial pigtail as well. (We discussed these because of oil wicking being a problem in wiring harnesses. — SM) What should […]
body_text: Anthony writes: “Hi! I am about to purchase a 2017 Mercedes S63 cabriolet with 42k miles. Is it a wise practice to drop the oils? Which oils specifically? I hear mention of adding a sacrificial pigtail as well. ( We discussed these because of oil wicking being a problem in wiring harnesses. — SM) What should I look out for, and what’s the best way to make this a smooth transaction? Thank you!” Sajeev answers: This is a great question, because its answer is almost as complicated as the vehicle we’re discussing. The cheapskate in me fears there is no way to have a smooth transaction with a flagship Mercedes product after 9-plus years on the road, but we have several tools to minimize the risk. The first and most important aspect is to get a late-model German specialty repair shop to perform a pre-purchase inspection on your behalf. The shorthand for this service is PPI , and it can save you a lot of money when negotiating the sales price. At that age and mileage, this S63 likely has a fair bit of deferred maintenance, or possibly a deferred repair because the previous owner lost interest and would prefer not to replace a part that suffered a pothole hit, or anything else that fails due to unexpected incidents on the road. PPIs can spot problems you won’t, and that’s why they are worth their weight in gold. Mercedes-Benz But you have a possible alternative to the PPI, or at least a good supplement to one, if you happen to be buying the car from a reputable dealer (who doesn’t flip cars purchased sight-unseen from dealer auctions). A dealer should be able to provide a clean CARFAX (or a similar service) as well as recent service invoices to justify the asking price. The paperwork should come from a Mercedes-Benz dealership, proving the car was serviced correctly and regularly. (Dealership servicing is generally the gold standard, but when in doubt, get the PPI.) With documentation in hand, you can do most of the remaining PPI yourself. Inspect for interior/exterior flaws, look for collision repair (overspray, missing hardware, etc.), test every power assist, cycle the power top several times, use everything in every menu on the dashboard’s screen, listen for problems on a test drive, make sure the sound system works and is playing through all the speakers, and so on. If something isn’t working, you can try lowering the price or just walk away. (Or you can just pay a professional for their time, hence the value of a PPI.) Let’s say this S63 passes muster, and the deal is to your liking. Next up is your concern about “dropping the oils” at this age. And this mileage, because at 42,000 miles. I suspect it needs a “B” service : After a little hunting in menus, I bet you can find that deadline on the dashboard. If you have the MCT 7-speed gearbox , it’s getting close to needing a fluid change, too. The 4-matic-equipped models might also need a transfer case service. If you don’t know a good European-savvy repair shop, consider this paragraph as your clarion call to address this situation. Amazon The aforementioned sacrificial pigtails (shown above) can be a good idea, but I don’t know if the issue applies to 2017 models. Instead of trying to verify the problem/solution, I would double down on finding a good local mechanic and asking them for their advice. You are gonna need experts in the trade to keep an S63 running in top form. Which brings up a final point: If indeed you are buying from a dealership, ask the aforementioned experts what aftermarket warranty company they like to work with. Consider getting their recommended warranty from the selling dealer, as I suspect a couple of ABC repairs will pay for it. Good luck with the purchase. These V-8 AMG flagships are beyond fantastic, but it will take a lot of legwork to protect your wallet from long-term stress. Have a question you’d like answered on Piston Slap? Send your queries to pistonslap@hagerty.com — give us as much detail as possible so we can help! Keep in mind this is a weekly column, so if you need an expedited answer, please tell me in your email. The post Piston Slap: Safely Purchasing an S63 Flagship? appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: Cosmic Rundown: Google Leadership Shakeup, Cloudflare OS, and Stateless MCP
summary: Daily developer news: Demis Hassabis and Jeff Dean leave Google. Cloudflare announces OS for agents. Simon Willison on stateless MCP. Surveillance tech and GPS jamming.
body_text: Google loses Demis Hassabis and Jeff Dean Two stories dominated the front page: Demis Hassabis is stepping down as Google DeepMind CEO , and Jeff Dean is leaving Alphabet entirely . Hassabis built DeepMind into the research lab behind AlphaFold, AlphaGo, and much of Google's foundational AI work. Dean has been at Google since 1999 and architected systems like MapReduce, BigTable, and TensorFlow. Losing both in the same week signals something significant about where Google's AI talent sees the next chapter of their careers. The Hacker News discussion on Hassabis speculated about whether this reflects internal tensions or simply the pull of starting something new. The Jeff Dean thread noted that Google's announcement about the next chapter of their AI momentum appeared the same day, framing the departures as part of a broader transition. For teams building on Google's AI stack, this raises practical questions about roadmap continuity. The people who designed these systems often carry context that documentation cannot capture. Cloudflare announces Cloudflare OS Cloudflare OS positions the edge network as an operating system for agents, apps, and work. The announcement describes a platform where AI agents can run at the edge, close to users, without provisioning traditional infrastructure. The discussion explored what this means for serverless architectures and whether Cloudflare is positioning itself as the runtime layer for the agent era. Several commenters noted the strategic timing: as AI agents become practical, the question of where they run becomes important. This connects directly to content infrastructure. If agents are going to create, update, and publish content, they need APIs that work at the speed and scale of edge computing. A headless CMS with a REST API becomes the data layer these agents write to. Stateless MCP changes the game Simon Willison wrote that stateless MCP has recaptured his interest , and the Hacker News thread became one of the most active discussions of the day. MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets AI coding assistants connect to external tools and data sources. The original protocol required maintaining state, which created complexity. The stateless version simplifies integration dramatically. For content teams, this matters because MCP is how AI tools like Claude, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot connect to your content. Cosmic offers an MCP server that exposes 18 tools for managing content through any MCP client. When your AI assistant can read and write to your CMS directly, the workflow between ideation and publication compresses. License plate surveillance enables pretextual stops 404 Media reported that police used Flock license plate readers to track a man across state lines, then created a pretextual traffic stop to search his car for marijuana. The discussion examined the Fourth Amendment implications and the expanding network of automated surveillance. Flock cameras are deployed by thousands of police departments, creating a distributed system that tracks vehicle movements at scale. The technical architecture is familiar: edge devices capture data, a central platform aggregates and queries it, and alerts trigger based on patterns. The debate is about what happens when that architecture is deployed for population-scale surveillance without meaningful oversight. Military GPS blocking may have caused plane crash Wired reported that a civilian plane crash in New Mexico may be connected to military GPS jamming exercises. The thread explored the tension between military testing and civilian aviation safety. GPS jamming is a known technique for testing weapons systems and training pilots to operate without satellite navigation. When those exercises overlap with civilian airspace, the consequences can be fatal. The investigation is ongoing, but the incident highlights how military infrastructure decisions affect civilian systems in ways that are not always visible. AI solving Erdos problems Quanta Magazine covered why legendary Erdos problems are falling to AI. The discussion debated whether this represents genuine mathematical progress or sophisticated pattern matching. Paul Erdos posed hundreds of problems over his career, offering cash prizes for solutions. AI systems are now solving some of these, raising questions about what it means for a machine to do mathematics. The consensus in the thread leaned toward viewing these as tools that augment human mathematicians rather than replace them. Quick hits Qwen 3.0 Image Pro launched on QwenCloud , continuing the rapid iteration in image generation models. Oracle halved its Always Free ARM limits , as reported on cnelecar . The discussion noted that free tier reductions often precede pricing changes. TIME is serving AI bots a different website with ads built in , according to Vincent Schmalbach's analysis. Publishers are experimenting with how to monetize AI-driven traffic. A new research paper argues LLMs can't jump , available on OpenReview . The thread debated the methodology and what the findings mean for AI capabilities. Building content infrastructure that keeps pace with these developments means choosing tools designed for the AI era. Cosmic's AI agents handle content generation while keeping humans accountable for what ships. The REST API works with any frontend, and the MCP server connects your CMS to AI coding assistants. Start building for free and see how modern content infrastructure supports the workflows these tools enable.

body_text: Papa Johns Announces Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results August 06, 2026 7:00 am EDT Download as PDF Related Documents Earnings Webcast Audio Non-GAAP Reconciliations PDF 10-Q HTML PDF XBRL Zip Updates Fiscal 2026 Outlook Global System-wide Restaurant Sales Decreased 4.8%(a) and Global Comparable Sales Decreased 5.7% North America Comparable Sales Decreased 8.3% and International Comparable Sales Increased 1.5% Diluted EPS of $0.24 and Adjusted Diluted EPS(b) of $0.46 Company Shifts Capital Allocation to Accelerate Transformation Strategy; Suspends Dividend LOUISVILLE, Ky.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Papa John’s International, Inc. (Nasdaq: PZZA) (“Papa Johns®”) (the “Company”) today announced financial results for the second quarter ended June 28, 2026. Highlights Global system-wide restaurant sales were $1.20 billion, a 4.8%(a) decrease compared with the prior year second quarter. North America comparable sales decreased 8.3% from a year ago as comparable sales from Domestic Company-owned restaurants were down 8.9% and North America franchised restaurants were down 8.2%; International comparable sales increased 1.5% compared with the prior year second quarter. Opened 50 new restaurants system-wide, comprised of 9 restaurant openings in North America and 41 restaurant openings in International markets. Net income was $9 million compared with $10 million in the prior year second quarter. Adjusted EBITDA(b) was flat year over year at $53 million. Diluted earnings per common share was $0.24 compared with $0.28 in the prior year second quarter; adjusted diluted earnings per common share(b) was $0.46 compared with $0.41 last year. (a) Growth rate excludes the impact of foreign currency. (b) Represents a Non-GAAP financial measure. See “Non-GAAP Financial Measures” for a reconciliation to the most comparable U.S. GAAP measures. CEO Commentary and Dividend “Second quarter results reflected continued momentum in our International business, where we delivered our seventh consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales, and ongoing headwinds in North America driven by the softer consumer environment, lower order volumes, and a highly promotional QSR marketplace,” said Todd Penegor, President and CEO. “While our transformation is taking longer than anticipated, we continue to execute our strategy with discipline and focus and are seeing encouraging progress, including a growing and highly engaged Papa Rewards membership, supply chain savings, and AI-driven improvements to the customer ordering experience. By accelerating investments to strengthen our competitive position, improve restaurant economics, and attract new customers, we can build an even stronger foundation to gain market share and drive sustainable long-term growth. Accordingly, the Board has decided to suspend the Company’s quarterly dividend beginning with the third quarter of 2026 so that we have greater flexibility to make these investments and maintain our strong balance sheet,” continued Penegor. “As we look ahead, we are confident that we have the right operating and capital allocation strategy in place to improve performance and create value for our shareholders, customers and franchisees,” Penegor concluded. Second Quarter 2026 Results Revenue: The revenue commentary that follows includes a discussion of the Company’s segment results. Total revenues of $482.4 million in the second quarter of 2026 decreased $46.8 million, or 8.8%, compared with the prior year period, reflecting lower performance in North America, slightly offset by improved performance internationally. The decrease in revenues was mostly attributable to a $37 million decline at our Domestic Company-owned restaurants primarily related to: 1) approximately $25 million of lower revenues compared with the comparable prior period related to 85 Domestic Company-owned restaurants that were refranchised in the fourth quarter of 2025 and 2) 8.9% lower comparable sales. North America Commissary revenues decreased $12 million, primarily due to lower volumes, partially offset by higher pricing. North America Franchising revenues decreased $3 million due to lower comparable sales at franchised restaurants. Revenues from All Other business units decreased $8 million, primarily reflecting lower advertising funds revenue and lower digital fees. These declines were partially offset by a $1 million increase in International revenues driven by improved performance. System-wide sales: Global system-wide restaurant sales were $1.20 billion, down 4.8%(b) compared with the prior year second quarter, as higher International comparable sales was more than offset by lower comparable sales in North America and a decline in global net restaurants on a trailing twelve month basis. North America system-wide sales decreased 8%(b) to $850.7 million and International system-wide sales increased 5%(b) to $347.2 million in the second quarter of 2026, both as compared with the prior year period. Net income: Second quarter Net income was $8.7 million, a $1.0 million decrease compared with the prior year second quarter. The decrease was primarily related to lower sales partially offset by lower cost of sales and lower G&A expenses. Cost of sales declined in part due to the fourth quarter 2025 refranchising transaction and lower transaction volumes at our Domestic Company-owned restaurants along with lower volumes and commodity deflation at our North America commissaries. G&A expenses decreased compared with the prior year second quarter primarily due to lower supplemental advertising and lower management and other compensation costs. Net income also reflects lower interest expense driven by lower average interest rates during the quarter and higher tax expense due to a shift in income between jurisdictions and lower projected tax credits compared with the second quarter of 2025. (a) Represents a Non-GAAP financial measure. See “Non-GAAP Financial Measures” for a reconciliation to the most comparable U.S. GAAP measures. (b) Growth rate excludes the impact of foreign currency. Adjusted EBITDA: Adjusted EBITDA(a) was $52.7 million, a $0.1 million increase from the prior year second quarter. The increase was primarily attributable to the aforementioned declines in cost of sales and G&A expenses and improved performance in our International markets, mostly offset by lower sales and volumes in North America, as compared with the second quarter of 2025. Earnings per share: Diluted earnings per common share was $0.24 for the second quarter of 2026 compared with $0.28 in the second quarter of 2025. Adjusted diluted earnings per common share(a) was $0.46 for the second quarter of 2026 compared with $0.41 in the second quarter of 2025. These changes were due to the same factors impacting Net income and adjusted EBITDA(a) discussed above. Cash Dividend The Company’s capital allocation priorities are guided by a framework that prioritizes investment in the business, maintaining a strong balance sheet, and returning capital to shareholders through share repurchases and dividends. Leveraging this framework and the Company’s commitment to allocating capital to the highest return opportunities, the Papa John’s Board of Directors voted to suspend the quarterly dividend, beginning with the third quarter 2026 dividend. This action will allow the Company to accelerate investment in its transformation strategy to grow share and deliver the greatest value for shareholders, including: franchise financial incentives tied to operational excellence and restaurant image improvements; new customer acquisition through a sharper aggregator strategy, addressable market expansion, product innovation, and core menu improvement; technology, such as the deployment of the new point-of-sale system; supply chain optimization to improve cost leverage and 4-wall EBITDA in restaurants; and investment to build on momentum in the International business. As the Company realizes the benefits from its transformation, the Board of Directors intends to revisit how to most effectively return capital to shareholders through share repurchases and dividends.
